title: Small Companies Working Together: You Bet and Neuhaus Metalworks – John Watson
content:
After the 2026 Made Bike Show, John swung through Nevada City, California, to hang with the team at You Bet! for a few days. While there, he attended a Neuhaus Metalworks happy hour and ride, and in between, a multi-day conversation led to the following reflection…

On my drive home from Made, I pinged my buddy Jay Barre in Nevada City to see if I could crash with him and his family for a few days. I’d be driving in from Oakridge and was looking forward to having zero obligations aside from some High Sierra riding and catching up with friends.

The following morning, Jay, Shane, and I met up to ride in the Tahoe National Forest, catching up on all things You Bet and soaking in the dusty high country. It turns out, it was my buddy Parker’s last week working at You Bet. To celebrate Parker’s departure, Whit from Meriwether, Parker, and Jay did Chimney Rock, a harrowing climb in the Downieville area. Fresh off a 5,000′ climb the day before, we kept the pace casual. The conversation focused on the shop, small businesses, and change.

Small Businesses

Running a small business these days, particularly in the bike industry, ain’t easy. Jay and Parker, along with Kurt, who’s been with You Bet since the beginning, have been cranking hard all summer at You Bet, ensuring people’s bikes get fixed and back on the trails, while dancing the delicate game of keeping the floor stocked with inventory and forecasting for the busiest time of the year.

I’ve spent the greater part of my life hanging out in bike shops. From being a young grom to spending time in various cities and, most recently, helping design a bike shop. While I have never owned a shop, I’ve been friends with various shop owners over the years and can say with certainty that most IBDs do not have it easy right now.

Commenting on the slim floor models in stock to Jay, we got into a discussion about how the bike shop model is changing, and how he believes his approach is for the better.

You Bet’s Changes

You Bet is based in Nevada City, California, a town of roughly 3,000 people, just north of Grass Valley, a city with 12,000 people, en route to pristine mountain biking in the Lost Sierra. The destination towns of Downieville, Tahoe, and Graeagle await endless gravel roads and singletrack. Most of the day-to-day customers are either coming up from the Bay Area en route to a riding destination, are seasonal, or are year-round locals.

In recent years, many shops have shifted from flipping floor models to custom, one-on-one builds, with an emphasis on streamlining service. Jay said the impetus was that bigger companies You Bet had carried in the past were too focused on preseason (pre-sale) orders and had sales reps completely detached from the local economy.

“We don’t do a pre-season,” Jay mentioned, referring to the pre-orders many brands use to help with demand forecasting for their model years. “A lot of brands have a broken, old model, and it just doesn’t work anymore. All the weight and stress is in the shops with stocking a full-size run of each model and color.” Having inventory might be easiest for the customer, but many brands have shifted to a direct-to-consumer pricing structure while requiring shops to take pre-season orders. It’s a lose-lose scenario for shops like You Bet.

Disconnected Brands

“Dealing with a sales rep is essentially dealing with someone twice removed from the company’s operations, who, oftentimes, is being lied to by their bosses. Versus a small company where you’re dealing with the owners directly.” Jay’s not alone in this rationale. Pushy reps can be detached from the reality most IBDs are facing.

“As a small shop owner, you have to have these convos with the brands, through their reps, and they don’t know the real-world situation with the economy…”

“They pretend to,” Parker chimes in.

Jay continues, “…and they have set expectations based on the COVID bubble. But the biggest frustration is the reps thinking they know more about the local markets than the shops themselves.”

We all just sat there in silence for a few minutes.

Thanks to Laurient from Velo Cosmos for letting me shoot this photo of the Neuhaus 32er and his Chevy C20…

Consumer Spending

Local markets have gotten pickier as the economy has been pinched by tariffs and other policies, weighing heavily on consumers, who fight for control in a sea of uncertainty by tightening their wallets.

Jay continued, “For us, it’s the equation of not doing a stocking order but still being a stocking dealer. We’ll then take click-and-collect orders from DTC sales while still having a few select models on the floor. That way, we can still sell bikes, but we just didn’t pre-book them.  Unfortunately, the margin will be smaller, but we’ve gotta run lean and have low overhead.”

Meanwhile, You Bet has shifted from the bigger, sales-rep-oriented companies to focus on smaller brands like Otso Cycles, Wilde Bikes, Sklar Bikes, and Neuhaus Metalworks, all of which offer models that are perfect for riding around the NorCal region surrounding You Bet.

You Bet can offer “OE+” build kits for frames like this Taiwan-made Neuhaus Hummingbird…

Frame Up Builds

I asked Jay, “So do you order a size run of frames from Neuhaus Metalworks and wait for the right customer?” Jay expanded, “Honestly, if we hang a frame on the wall, it’ll just sit there, and no one will buy it… But then we’ll put a bike together with a particular budget in mind, and the customer will see it and want it, but in their size or a different color option.” From there, it’s a phone call to the bike company and a conversation with the customer about the build spec.

All this takes more time than walking up and buying a floor model, but it lets the customer spec exactly what they want. Perhaps they’ll go with an entry-level suspension fork and spring for better wheels, or cable shifting over electric, and so on.

This curation of builds resonates with Jay and his customers. In many ways, they reflect Jay’s personal taste while balancing availability, reliability, and serviceability, and addressing local economic or environmental riding demands. “It’s just my taste that builds the bikes, and I think it’s what customers value over here. A lot of the time, it’s different from what companies offer as stock builds, too.”

Currently, Jay has a few Neuhaus frames on display and a sick size large Sklar Super Something built with that limited-edition Shimano Cues kit. “Sometimes people do buy a frame because we’ll happen to have it in stock.” There’s also a size large salmon colored Sklar PBJ on display, but as we’re talking, a local calls up and buys it then and there over the phone. “That’s crazy…” Jay says, laughing. “See?” He says.

Mac, Nick, and Alex from Neuhaus…

Small Bike Shops and Brands

The model, while tenuous and time-consuming, seems to be working for You Bet and, if anything, offers a bit of sanity to small IBDs. Having personal relationships with these small bike brands goes a long way.

“When you call one of these smaller companies, you’re dealing with someone up at the top, often the owner of the company,” he continued. “I can call Adam Sklar or Nick Neuhaus and have a frame here in a day or so since they’re local California companies.” “Or I can call up Otso and have the exact bike in an OE build spec that the customer wants in under a week.”

Working with small brands, as a small shop, means there’s more transparency, too. “From a business standpoint, they’re super honest and transparent,” noting how small businesses have stuck together through the post-COVID pandemic cycling industry bubble. “Nick or Daniel at Neuhaus will be like, ‘The ship’s a week out, and we can have your frames to you in about two to three weeks…’ it’s just so refreshing.” Jay values this kind of honesty, and it makes it easy to set expectations with his customers.

Neuhaus might not be as well known as Otso Cycles, so Jay likes to have “hands-on” events for his local customers, or anyone who happens to be in town. These happy hour Friday parties make it easy for people to test ride bikes and meet the brand’s designer or owner. “One day, I just asked Nick if we could do an open house-style meet-and-greet happy hour at the shop. He was stoked, and we made it happen. It’s just so easy.”

Showing up after the Made Bike Show, the last thing I wanted to do that weekend was talk or shoot bikes, but my circle of friends has repeated these conversations so often that they really resonated with me. Friday afternoon arrived and with it, the Neuhaus crew. Nick, Mac, and Alex showed up in their van and unloaded bikes into the You Bet parking lot, while Junie, Parker’s dog, sat and surveyed the scene. Jay bought chips, cheesy bread from the local pizza shop, and rolled out a keg of beer from the local brewery.

Neuhaus Metalworks Happy Hour and Ride

People showed up, test-rode bikes, and talked shop. A beautiful, cloud-filled evening arrived, and I got to catch up with some long-time friends who’d moved to Nevada City after the Eaton Fire in Los Angeles. I even got to ride some Neuhaus models myself. All this happened with one simple phone call, a calendar date, and a loose plan. I just so happened to be there. The following morning, we discussed doing a small ride. And yes, I couldn’t help but bring along a camera for the ride.

The following morning, we all met up for a group ride, and after post-ride pizza, we all parted ways. I had a long drive ahead of me the following day, and many of our conversations ruminated as I passed through the Basin and Range Province along Highway 50, the Loneliest Highway. Loneliness made for ample time for reflection, as my car was pelted with a proper monsoon deluge on my drive home. The West is parched this year, and while the struggles of the independent bike dealers span the globe, I feel that a storm of change is blowing in.

Small companies working with small shops seem to be a bastion of safety for shops like You Bet. As the industry still grapples with a post-COVID world, there’s solace in small brands looking out for each other. There’s also friendship, which spawns words of encouragement and support. But the market is still tough.

For bike media like The Radavist, we feel this pain all too acutely. Which is why we encourage you to sign up as a Supporting Member.
